cim: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process
cim_eredeti: AI can help — or engulf — the legal process
szoveg_eredeti:
Cedar Rapids lawyer Tim Semelroth gives a presentation on artificial intelligence in 2025 at the University of Iowa College of Law. Semelroth wrote his first article in the American Bar Association Journal three years ago about the practical uses of AI by lawyers. Since then, he’s given more than 30 presentations around the country about the pros — and cons — of the technology.

CEDAR RAPIDS — A Cedar Rapids lawyer is encouraging his colleagues and the general public to think of AI as “Average Intelligence,” given the well-publicized “hallucinations” it has created in legal briefs and other papers.

Though the examples are head-shakingly humorous, AI is causing real problems in the legal system, says Tim Semelroth, who is teaching those in the legal profession about the use of AI technology.

That’s because no matter how “frivolous or without merit” AI-generated legal filings might be, lawyers have to review them and judges have to rule on them — costing time and money.

The problem with AI, he said, is that it’s been trained on the internet, where a lot of misinformation and bad legal opinions live. AI can’t distinguish between that “slop” and legitimate cases.

“It’s difficult because it’s the nature of AI,” said Semelroth, a medical malpractice and personal injury lawyer. “Every AI tool is trained to give people what they want. It gets to know you and is trained to please you. This is why it’s a bad research tool because if it can’t find answer, it will come up with a best guess based on everything else.

“It’s going out and trying to predict what the next word, letter and image that will be based on what came before it,” he said.

Some 2,000 examples of “hallucinated” filings have been reported, leading judges to sanction the lawyers who have filed the time-consuming briefs.

“If judges are encountering 100-page, ChatGPT-generated briefs, the system is going to grind to a halt,” Semelroth said.

Lawyers, he added, have an ethical responsibility to understand AI technology and make sure the information it provides is accurate because everyone around them — including their clients — are using it some way.

The clients may be asking AI about a legal defense or an opinion they found in ChatGPT. A witness may use an AI tool to generate a report in preparation for testifying. Law firm staff members may use it for research. So lawyers need to have security and policies in place.

“Not talking to staff about AI is like not talking to your teenagers about sex,” Semelroth said. “Just because you don’t have a discussion, doesn’t mean it’s not going to happen. AI is a powerful tool that can be good, but there are responsibilities that come with it.”

Semelroth wrote his first article in the American Bar Association Journal three years ago about the practical uses of AI. Since then, as the use of AI increased, he’s given more than 30 presentations around the country on the technology.

Cedar Rapids lawyer Tim Semelroth gives a presentation on artificial intelligence in July at the American Association for Justice convention in Chicago.

One point worth noting: There is a difference between a free AI tool and a subscription AI version, which is what lawyers use because the subscription models require safety protocols. But even those aren’t fail-safe.

“Nothing AI generates should leave your office without being checked by a human being,” Semelroth always tells lawyers.

During his presentations, Semelroth shows his audiences a slide with the Terminator and Ironman, asking which they prefer. He tries to persuade lawyers they want to be Ironman because “a human is involved” in his actions.

In his artificial intelligence talks, Cedar Rapids lawyer Tim Semelroth shows this slide, asking lawyers in the audience if they want to be the Terminator (left) or Ironman. He argues in favor of Ironman because "a human is involved,” something he encourages lawyers to remember to include when working with AI.

For lay people, artificial intelligence presents more of a challenge, even danger, because most people don’t have a way to verify the information AI is giving them, Semelroth said.

People may use AI to seek legal advice or research a legal defense if they are facing criminal charges. But that research has no privacy guarantees, and a person could be required to turn over their search information to prosecutors or the opposing side.

Semelroth cites one New York case where an individual believed he was going to be charged with a crime, so he started a chat on an AI app about his options and possible defenses. The prosecution found out, and a judge ruled prosecutors had the right to see the man’s chat history. The defendant had no right to privacy.

“In terms of the public, I would say please don’t try to use an AI tool for legal advice,” Semelroth said.

Semelroth said talking with a lawyer provides confidentiality, as opposed to consulting a chatbot.

The Iowa Supreme Court recently issued its first AI-related ruling in a case out of Woodbury County District Court in northwest Iowa.

A defendant, Max Amyda, 37, was convicted of third-degree sexual abuse in 2023. He appealed, claiming video evidence depicting him sexually assaulting the victim was AI-generated — a “deepfake.”

He argued the district court should have rejected that evidence because it wasn’t properly authenticated and it was a copy — not the original. The district court denied his argument.

The Iowa Court of Appeals upheld his conviction, stating circumstantial evidence based on “distinctive characteristics” — the victim, during testimony, identified her body and items in her room in the video, and she recognized Amyda’s hand touching her — which were sufficient to find the video is a depiction of Amyda sexually assaulting the victim.

The appeals court also rejected Amyda’s argument regarding it not being the original video. The video still is admissible as a duplicate because Amyda’s “speculative claims” that the video is a “deepfake” were without any evidence and he didn’t raise a genuine question about its authenticity.

Amyda asked the Iowa Supreme Court for a further review, and it affirmed the appeals ruling Oct. 9.

The justices ruled Amyda’s argument was based only on “conjecture,” Semelroth said. The video was correctly admitted into evidence because the distinctive characteristics in the video were sufficient for it to be considered authentic and shown to the jury.

Semelroth said much discussion is going on in the legal community about whether the rules of evidence and legal procedure can withstand the use of AI and allegations of “deepfakes” by the public and lawyers.

The Iowa Supreme Court ruling in the Woodbury County case — regarding whether evidence could be used in court when someone argues it might be an AI-generated “deepfake” — has provided more guidance for lawyers, he said.

In July, the Iowa Supreme Court also took action to put rules in place for judges and staff using AI tools.

Chief Justice Susan Christensen signed an order adopting a new chapter of the Iowa Court Rules — Judicial Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools.

Semelroth was on the 25-member working group appointed by the court last year to develop internal policies and procedures for the technology use by judicial officers and to evaluate potential applications that could be used in court operations.

As part of the new rules, a Judicial Branch Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Governance Committee evolved from the working group Semelroth was on.

The committee will provide oversight as the courts evaluate emerging technologies and determine how the tools will be used by judges and other staff. Judges, court administrators, court reporters, IT staff, two law professors and other judicial staff on the committee.
